_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: In the middle of the Jubilee: that is, this “after” [the Jubilee] stands even after twenty or thirty years. And what is the “less than a year” that it says? This is what it means: one who comes to redeem in the middle of the Jubilee [cycle], to give a sela and a pundeyon for the coming years, and he was standing in Nisan, which is the middle of the year, may not say: I give half a sela and half a pundeyon for this year; rather, he gives a whole sela and pundeyon. And this is what it says: one does not redeem for less than a year, for as long as the whole year has not gone out, nothing is deducted for it at all, and he does not give the redemption of half a year but the redemption of a full year.
rashi:a2.1: [That one does not count months with the Temple: as we said, that if he comes to redeem it five and a half years before the Jubilee, one does not count for him those six months that have gone out of the year into the sixth year; rather, he gives six sela and six pundeyon.]
rashi:a3.1: The years that remain: whatever remains counts as years.
rashi:a4.1: To make months a year: to count those months that have gone out as if they were a year, and that is its [the Temple’s] gain.
rashi:a4.2: And what are the circumstances? Where he consecrated it in the middle of the forty-eighth [year]: for if you count the months that have gone out as fully gone out, there are less than two years [left], and it is not redeemed with a deduction.
rashi:a6.1: Mishna. At the time of the Jubilee: when the Jubilee is in force. But when the Jubilee is not in force, one redeems it at its value, like other consecrated property.
rashi:a6.2: They are not measured with it: and they are redeemed at their value, and the rest according to the reckoning of fifty sela per beit kor.
rashi:a7.1: And any person: redeems a beit ḥomer for fifty shekels, whether it is worth a thousand shekels or worth only five shekels.
rashi:a7.2: That the owner gives a fifth: as it is written: “And if he that sanctified the field will indeed redeem it” and so on [“then he shall add the fifth part of the money,” Leviticus 27:19].
rashi:a8.1: Gemara. A kor of seed: in which one can sow a kor.
rashi:a8.2: And not a kor of crop: ground from which one reaps a kor of crop, which is much smaller than a kor of seed; for that one does not require fifty, but according to the reckoning of the seed, a third of a kor or a quarter of a kor.
rashi:a8.3: The falling of the hand: that one sows by hand.
rashi:a8.4: And not the falling of oxen: they used to put sacks full of seed on the oxen, the sacks pierced underneath with wide holes, and lead them along the plow, and the seed falls. And ground that takes a kor of seed sown by the falling of the hand, which is not dense, is larger than ground that takes a kor of seed sown by the falling of oxen, which is dense.
rashi:a8.5: It is taught: one does not measure by densely sown seed, which is the loss of the one who redeems;
rashi:a8.6: Nor: by sparse seed, which is a loss to the Temple, since that would be a large beit kor; but by average sowing.
rashi:a8.7: Dense: where much seed is put in. Sparse: where little seed is put in. (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:a9.1: And let them be consecrated: these crevices by themselves, and let them also be redeemed according to the reckoning of fifty per beit kor. And what benefit is there in their not being measured with it? They too are redeemed in just this way!
rashi:a10.1: “Field”, why must the verse state it? It could have written: “And if a man shall sanctify part of his ancestral possession,” and so on.
rashi:a10.2: In this manner: a full beit kor.
rashi:a10.4: Tarkav: half a se’a; “two and a kav” [tarei-kav], that is, three kav, which are half a se’a.
rashi:a12.1: Negani: crevices less than ten [handbreadths]. Negani de’ara are basins of the ground where the water gathers; they are named after the ground and are not considered by themselves. And boulders lower than ten are called spines of the ground, like the spine of an animal, which is raised.
rashi:a14.1: Even from the consecration: just as it is deducted for those years in which it stood in his possession when he had not consecrated it, so too it is deducted for those years in which it stood in the possession of the Temple, from the time of consecration until the time of redemption.
rashi:a14.2: Or even if it did not consume it: the treasurer did not sow anything in it and did not rent it out to anyone, but it was before him in the possession of the Temple; he deducts a sela and a pundeyon for each and every year from the Jubilee that passed until the time of redemption.
rashi:a16.1: Mishna. It does not leave his possession in the Jubilee: to be divided among the priests, as it would if another person had redeemed it, when it would leave in the Jubilee to be divided among the priests, as it is written: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee” and so on (Leviticus 27:21).
rashi:a16.2: His son redeemed it, it goes out to his father in the Jubilee: and not to the priests, as is derived in the baraita in the Gemara.
rashi:a16.3: One of his relatives redeemed it: from the treasurer, and the one who consecrated it came and redeemed it from his relative’s possession: it goes out in the Jubilee and is divided among the priests, just as it would have gone out of that relative’s possession, since this one came [to hold it] through him.
rashi:a17.1: A priest redeemed it: from the treasurer. He may not say: Since, had an Israelite redeemed it, it would go out to me and my fellows in the Jubilee, and now it is in my possession, for I redeemed it, there is no priest with a greater claim than I, so let it be mine.
tosafot:a4.1: Where he consecrated it in the middle of the forty-eighth: “consecrated” is not meant precisely, for the matter does not depend on the consecration but only on the redemption.
tosafot:a9.1: And let them be consecrated by themselves: I have explained this in Bava Batra (103a) and Kiddushin (61a).
gershom:a1.1: As long as the year is not complete, nothing is deducted for it: that is, if it was in the possession of the Temple five and a half years and he comes to redeem it, he may not say: for those five and a half years that it was in the possession of the Temple I will deduct six shekels and six pundeyon against it, counting the half year as if it were complete. Rather, he counts it with the years remaining until the Jubilee, to give the Temple a sela and a pundeyon a year for it.
gershom:a2.1: What is he teaching us, that one does not count months with the Temple? That is, that if he consecrated it and redeemed it after half a year, he does not deduct against the Temple for it half a sela and half a pundeyon.
gershom:a3.1: But it is taught explicitly: that one does not count [months] at all.
gershom:a4.1: Rav will tell you: yes, it is one matter, and it is stating “what is the reason.” Therefore, at any rate, there is no inference to be drawn to exclude the Jubilee Year itself.
gershom:a5.1: One does not count months for the Temple: he may not count against the Temple for half a year or eight months, as if he had consecrated it at the end of the year, to reduce a sela and a pundeyon against them, or against the months that passed, as is taught in the baraita. Complete years in which it was not [in the Temple’s possession] you count, to reduce a sela and a pundeyon against them, but not against months. But the Temple counts months as a year, as is explained in the Gemara: for example, where he consecrated it in the middle of the forty-eighth. For it might enter your mind: what we say, that one does not consecrate [so as] to redeem with a deduction less than two years before the Jubilee, applies when he consecrated it at the end of the forty-eighth; but when he consecrated it in the middle of the forty-eighth, let us say it is as though he consecrated it at the beginning of the forty-eighth, which is two years before the Jubilee, and it is redeemed with a deduction. It teaches us that we make these months a year, as though he consecrated it at the end of the forty-eighth, for the Temple’s gain, so that he does not redeem with a deduction but gives fifty shekels to the Temple; and this is “but the Temple counts months as a year.” And likewise, if it stood in the Temple’s possession ten and a half years, the one who consecrated it counts only ten years, and that half year he counts as a full year with the remaining years, and for that half year too he gives a sela and a pundeyon, like a full year, with the years remaining until the Jubilee.
gershom:a6.1: The verse states: “Then the priest shall reckon for him,” in any case: that he reckons so that there is gain for the Temple.
gershom:a7.1: At the time of the Jubilee: when the Jubilee is in force.
gershom:a8.1: He gives: right after the Jubilee, when he redeems it from [the Temple], he gives fifty shekels [for the sowing of] a ḥomer of barley.
gershom:a9.1: A kor of seed and not a kor of crop: that is, when he measures how many kor are in it, he measures by the area fit to sow a kor in it, which is more than an area in which a kor of crop can grow, since a grain of seed makes an ear of grain. And this is the gain of the one who consecrated it, for if it went by a kor of crop he would give many shekels; rather, it goes by a kor of seed.
gershom:a10.1: A kor of seed: sown by the falling of the hand and not sown by the falling of oxen. [For this is how they sowed by the falling of oxen:] they would fill a sack [full of grain] and set it on the cart over the container, and in the container there was a hole; the cart would be drawn along the furrow and the grain would fall through that hole, and so they sowed with oxen. Now one who sows by hand scatters the seed more, and a beit kor of seed sown by hand takes up a larger area of the field than by oxen, because it [sowing by oxen] does not sow evenly: sometimes much falls together from the hole and sometimes little of the seed falls.
gershom:a11.1: Levi taught: [about] the falling of the hand that they spoke of.
gershom:a12.1: Not dense: where much is dropped together, which is the loss of the one who consecrated it, since the kors would multiply.
gershom:a13.1: Nor sparse: where he scatters too widely, which is a loss to the Temple, since it reduces the kors; rather, average.
gershom:a14.1: They are not measured with it: because they are a domain of their own.
gershom:a15.1: “Field”, why must the verse state it? [It could have] written: “And if of his ancestral possession he shall sanctify.”
gershom:a16.1: In this manner: in this measure, the sowing of a ḥomer of barley for fifty.
gershom:a17.1: From where: if he consecrated a field of a letekh or half a letekh, that he must redeem it.
gershom:a18.1: The verse states “field”, in any case: that it is consecrated.
gershom:a19.1: Similar to boulders: which are not fit for sowing.
gershom:a20.1: If so: since we have interpreted it as crevices full of water, why are those less than this measured with it?
gershom:a21.1: Because they are called cracks of the ground: basins of the field in which water is placed to irrigate it, and they are considered as field. And likewise boulders less than ten [(an Old French gloss)] are called spines of the ground, for many such are found in fields, and they are considered as field.
gershom:a22.1: “And a deduction shall be made from your valuation,” even from the consecration: that is, just as [if he consecrated it ten years after the Jubilee and redeemed it at the end of twenty, they deduct for him] those years that it was in the owner’s possession, for which he does not give a sela and a pundeyon, so if the Temple consumed it a year or two [or ten], they deduct for him a sela and a pundeyon for all those years that it was in the Temple’s possession, and he gives a sela and a pundeyon only for the years after the redemption within the Jubilee [cycle].
gershom:a23.1: And if he said: I will give for each year during the year: a sela and a pundeyon each year, one does not listen to him [as it is said: “Then the priest shall reckon for him the money,” how much it comes to for him to give until the Jubilee, and they give it together].
gershom:a24.1: Both the owner and any person: may redeem the sowing of a ḥomer of barley for fifty shekels.
gershom:a25.1: Only that the owner: adds a fifth on top of the fifty shekels, as it is said: “And if he that sanctified the field will indeed redeem it, then he shall add the fifth part of the money” (Leviticus 27:19).
gershom:a26.1: His son redeemed it: in his place.
gershom:a27.1: It goes out to his father in the Jubilee: and does not go out to the priests. [A printer’s note suggests reading: and it is as though he himself redeemed it.] (And it does not come to that one himself [the son].)
gershom:a28.1: Another or one of the relatives redeemed it: and this one who consecrated it went back and redeemed it from his possession, it goes out of his possession in the Jubilee. [The printed text has “does not” before “go out” in parentheses, marking it as an error.]
rashi:b3.1: Gemara. To another man: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee” [shall be] for the priests.
rashi:b3.2: And not to the son: for if his son redeemed it, it does not go out to the priests but to his father.
rashi:b3.3: The brother is stated: that he is like another, and it goes out to the priests.
rashi:b4.1: For designation: if his father bought a Hebrew maidservant and he [the son] wants to designate her for himself, he designates her; he need not betroth her with other money, but with that same money his father gave for her when he bought her she is betrothed to him, as is explained in the first chapter of Kiddushin (19b).
rashi:b4.2: And for a Hebrew slave: he serves the son if his master died within the six years, but he does not serve the brother: if his master died without a son and his brother inherits him, he does not serve him, as we say in the first chapter of Kiddushin (17b). So too we set the son in place of the father for an ancestral field: just as it does not leave his father’s possession to be divided among the priests [when the father redeems it], if his son redeemed it, it does not go out to the priests in the Jubilee.
rashi:b6.1: And let him derive it from the fact that here there are two, and so on: and he would not need to answer: Is there ever levirate marriage, and so on.
rashi:b7.1: Because: that the son stands in place of his father for a Hebrew slave is derived for us not from a verse but from this refutation, “Is there ever levirate marriage,” and so on, as we say in Kiddushin (17b): What did you see to include the son for a Hebrew slave and to exclude the brother? I include the son, as he stands in place of his father for designation. On the contrary, I include the brother, as he stands in place of his brother for levirate marriage. And it answers: Is there ever levirate marriage other than where there is no son? And were it not for this refutation, “Is there ever levirate marriage,” and so on, he would not have derived it for a Hebrew slave, and it would be one here and one there.
rashi:b8.1: What is the halakha with regard to whether she preserves, and so on: if his daughter redeemed an ancestral field from the treasurer, what is the halakha with regard to whether it goes out to her father in the Jubilee and not to the priests?
rashi:b9.1: Anyone who is another in the place of a son: where there is a son, this one is considered like another and does not preserve it.
rashi:b10.1: A woman: who consecrated a field of her usufruct property [milog]: who may redeem it from the Temple so that it does not go out to the priests in the Jubilee, if she herself cannot redeem it?
rashi:b10.2: As he inherits her: for he inherits her even if she has a son; her husband inherits her and not the son, as it is written: “and he shall inherit it” [Numbers 27:11], which teaches that the husband inherits his wife (Bava Batra 111b).
rashi:b10.3: Or perhaps the son preserves it for her: for where there is no husband and her son inherits her, he takes property due to fall to her after death as he does property held before death; but a husband who inherits his wife does not take what is due as he does what is held, as we say in the chapter Yesh Noḥalin (Bava Batra 113a).
rashi:b11.1: He consecrated it less than two years before the Jubilee: and another came and redeemed it, not with a deduction but for a full fifty. What is the halakha with regard to whether it goes out to the priests in the Jubilee like any ancestral field? [Rashi reads the case as one where another person redeemed the field; the Davidson English speaks of a field that was not redeemed.]
rashi:b12.1: What is your reasoning: that you would want to say it does not go out.
rashi:b15.1: With regard to a field that goes out to the priests: one fit to be given to the priests in the Jubilee, which the owner consecrated and did not redeem.
rashi:b15.2: And one of the priests redeemed it: from the treasurer.
rashi:b15.3: I acquire [fields] of others: had an Israelite redeemed it, it would go out of his possession and I would acquire it with the rest of my brethren.
rashi:b16.1: The verse states: “His ancestral possession shall be for the priest”: it can be expounded thus: the ancestral possession of a priest, which he inherited from his father, shall be his; but this one is not his.
rashi:b17.1: Mishna. The priests enter into it, and so on: the priests of the [priestly] watch [serving] at the Jubilee enter into it, and so on, and it is permanently theirs.
rashi:b18.1: An abandoned field: left alone until another redeems it, and when the Jubilee arrives it goes out of his possession to the priests.
rashi:b19.1: Gemara. From one who consecrates a house: regarding one who consecrates a house it is written (Leviticus 27:14): “When a man shall sanctify his house to be holy,” and regarding an ancestral field it is written: “when it goes out in the Jubilee, holy,” and so on [Leviticus 27:21]. Just as a house never leaves the Temple’s possession without money, as it is written there: “Then the priest shall value it,” and so on (and a house never goes out to the priests; only an ancestral field does, for it is a royal decree), so too an ancestral field does not leave the Temple’s possession without money. Therefore, when another redeems it, its money has gone to Temple maintenance, and when the Jubilee arrives it goes out to the priests for free; and if it was not redeemed, the priests give its money, fifty shekels, and take it.
rashi:b21.1: Regarding the lambs of Shavuot it is written (Leviticus 23:20–21): “They shall be holy to the Lord for the priest.” The lambs of Shavuot and the ancestral field are among the twenty-four gifts of the priesthood (Numbers 18), but a house never belongs to the priests, even if another redeemed it from the Temple.
tosafot:b4.1: (Belongs to amud b.) For designation and for a Hebrew slave: And if you say: why does it not also count inheritance? One cannot say it is because we know [the son’s precedence in] inheritance only by this reasoning, that he precedes for an ancestral field, as is found in the chapter Yesh Noḥalin (Bava Batra 108b). That is not so, for even if they were equal in other matters, such as a Hebrew slave and an ancestral field, in any case for designation the son precedes the brother explicitly in the verse, and from it we know inheritance well. Therefore it seems right to explain that it mentions only matters that do not apply to a brother at all; but inheritance does apply to a brother, at least where there is neither son nor daughter (nor father).
tosafot:b5.1: Is there ever levirate marriage other than where there is no son? Meaning: and the son is preferable to the brother in this matter. But one should not explain, as it appears at first glance, that they are equal in this matter and so the son is preferable through designation and the Hebrew slave. For that is not how it appears in Yesh Noḥalin (Bava Batra 109a), which concludes that a daughter precedes the father and the brother for this very reason: with regard to levirate marriage a son and a daughter are alike, so with regard to inheritance too a son and a daughter are alike. Evidently we must say that for this reason the son is preferable to the brother.
tosafot:b16.1: In brief: Tosafot ask why the word “his ancestral possession” is needed at all, since the a fortiori argument could be refuted without a verse, as at the end of this tractate regarding a field of dedications, where a similar a fortiori is rejected: there the priest merely acquires in general, here he takes it [into his own hands]. They answer that without “his ancestral possession” one would have derived, by the verbal analogy “priest”–“priest” from property stolen from a convert, that the field does not leave the priest’s possession. So the passage in Bava Kamma (109b) shows: a baraita asks, where a priest robbed a convert [who died without heirs], from where do we know that he may not say: since it goes out to the priests and it is in my possession, let it be mine? It is logical: if I acquire what is others’, all the more so what is mine. And it is written: “And every man’s hallowed things shall be his” [Numbers 5:10], from which it is derived that a priest may offer his own offerings whenever he wishes, even in a watch not his own; so he should offer his guilt offering for robbing the convert and keep the principal as well. The Gemara there answers that we derive “priest”–“priest” from an ancestral field, which goes out of his possession and is divided among all his brethren the priests, and to show the source for that it cites this passage. Evidently, were it not for “his ancestral possession,” one would have said that the convert’s stolen property does not leave the priest’s possession because of “every man’s hallowed things shall be his,” and one would have derived that the ancestral field too does not leave the priest’s possession. That is why “his ancestral possession: it is his, and this is not his” is needed, and the convert’s stolen property is derived from it by the verbal analogy “priest”–“priest.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b20.1: Just as there it is by money, so too here by money: And if you say: from where do we know that the priests have more claim to it than another? Perhaps it is like one who consecrates a house, which goes out for money to whoever wishes, priest and Israelite alike; so too we should say here. One can say that the plain meaning of the verse implies it to him: “And if he will not redeem the field,” meaning the owner, but it stands in the treasurer’s possession until the Jubilee; “or if he sold the field to another man,” meaning another redeemed it: in these two ways the owner shall not redeem it again from the Temple, but rather “the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee, shall be holy to the Lord … for the priest.” Evidently the verses imply that it goes out into the priests’ possession, and the verbal analogy comes, for Rabbi Yehuda, to teach that it goes out for money and not for free, where another did not redeem it.
tosafot:b21.1: And Rabbi Shimon, what is the reason? This is puzzling: at first the Gemara asks what is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda, implying that Rabbi Shimon’s view is more plausible without a verbal analogy, and afterward it asks what is the reason of Rabbi Shimon, implying that Rabbi Yehuda’s is more plausible. One can say that we find the like in Bava Kamma (10b), regarding ten people who struck a man with ten sticks: to one Sage [the verse] “when he strikes any soul” implies until he strikes the whole soul, and to the other it implies any bit of soul. And it seems to me that according to what I explained it is well: the plain meaning of the verse implies that it goes out to the priests, and no verbal analogy would be needed to say that it goes out for money; and for the other Sage a verbal analogy is needed [to teach] that it goes out for free.
gershom:b1.1: The one who consecrated it did not redeem it, and one of the priests redeemed it, and it is in his possession at the Jubilee: he may not say, and so on.
gershom:b2.1: “And if he sold the field”: the treasurer, “to another man, it shall not be redeemed anymore” by the owner, but it returns to the priests in the Jubilee.
gershom:b3.1: To another and not to the son: for if the treasurer sold it to the son of the one who consecrated it, it returns to his father in the Jubilee.
gershom:b4.1: When it says “man”: unqualified, it implies his brother, [so that] it shall not be redeemed anymore.
gershom:b5.1: Why must the verse state “another”? To another it shall not be redeemed, but not to the son.
gershom:b6.1: [For designation: as it is written: “And if he designates her for his son” (Exodus 21:9).
gershom:b7.1: [A printer’s note: it seems it should read: Because of the Hebrew slave; that is why it does not object “here there are two and here levirate marriage alone,” because the Hebrew slave, and so on.] And for a Hebrew slave; and here, levirate marriage alone. That is why it does not object “here there are two,” because the Hebrew slave is derived from this refutation, “Is there ever,” and so on; it is from there that it is included. For so we learn in tractate Kiddushin: a Hebrew slave serves the son and not the brother. Do you say the son, or perhaps the brother and not the son? I include the son, who stands in place of his father for designation and for an ancestral field. On the contrary, I include the brother, who stands in place of (his father) [his brother] for levirate marriage. And we refute that “on the contrary” and say: Is there ever levirate marriage other than where there is no son? So where there is a son there is no levirate marriage. And from there the Hebrew slave is included, that the son stands in place of his father for a Hebrew slave; for we found a verse that he stands in his place only for designation alone. Therefore one cannot object “let him derive it from the fact that there it is two,” since we did not find a verse for both, only this refutation, “Is there levirate marriage where there is a son,” and it is like one against one.
gershom:b8.1: A daughter, what is the halakha with regard to whether she preserves: that is, if his daughter redeemed it, what is the halakha with regard to whether she preserves the field for her father, so that it returns to him in the Jubilee?]
gershom:b9.1: Since a daughter in the place of a son is like another: so too when she is not in the place of a son, she does not preserve the [field] for her father.
gershom:b10.1: (A woman who consecrated a field, [the treasurer] sold it to her [sic], and her husband redeemed it: does her husband preserve the field for her, so that it is hers in the Jubilee? Do we consider it as though she herself redeemed it?)
gershom:b11.1: [A woman who consecrated her usufruct field and her husband redeemed it: does her husband preserve the field for her, so that it is hers in the Jubilee? Do we consider it as though she herself redeemed it?]
gershom:b12.1: As the son takes what is due as what is held, as is explained in Yesh Noḥalin; and the son’s power is greater than the father’s.
gershom:b13.1: [For one that is not fit for deduction does not go out to the priests, since for less than two years one does not deduct but gives fifty shekels.]
gershom:b14.1: And this too is fit for redemption: [and if he did not redeem it,] it goes out to the priests.
gershom:b15.1: “His ancestral possession”, why must the verse state it? [It could have written:] “shall be for the priest.”
gershom:b16.1: With regard to a field that goes out to the priests: one that neither the owner nor his son redeemed, but a priest or another, so that it goes out to the priests in the Jubilee: from where do we know that he may not say, and so on.
gershom:b17.1: “His ancestral possession”: his own is his.
gershom:b18.1: And this is not his: alone. How so, and so on.
gershom:b19.1: The priests enter into it: as it is written: “shall be for the priest.”
gershom:b20.1: And give its value: to the Temple, as it is written: “holy to the Lord.”
gershom:b21.1: Rather, it is called an abandoned field: a field left lying, in which no one has any right, as it is written: “you shall let it rest and lie fallow [unetashtah]” [Exodus 23:11], which the Aramaic translation renders “and leave it abandoned [vetirteshinah]”, [until the second Jubilee].
gershom:b22.1: Abandoned of the abandoned: no one may touch it until the third Jubilee, for the priests never enter into it until another redeems it from the treasurer, as it is written: “or if he sold the field” (the treasurer) “to another man, it shall not be redeemed anymore” by the owner, but “the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee” [shall be for the priest].
gershom:b23.1: What is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda: who says here “and they give its value.”
gershom:b24.1: [It is written here: “holy to the Lord, as a dedicated field,” and it is written: “And when a man shall sanctify his house to be holy.”] Just as there [with a house] it is by money, as it is written: “he shall add the fifth part of the money” [Leviticus 27:15], [so too here by money.
gershom:b25.1: From the lambs of Shavuot: of which it is written: “They shall be holy to the Lord for the priest,” for free.]
gershom:b26.1: One derives items consecrated for Temple maintenance, and so on: for both a house and the value of an ancestral field are items consecrated for Temple maintenance.
gershom:b27.1: An ancestral field and the lambs of Shavuot are a gift to the priests, for of both it is written “shall be for the priest,” but not of one who consecrates a house. [This note explains the Gemara’s next answer, on 26a.]
